    42	\section{Key theorem forms}
    43	
    44	Let $S$ and $T$ be binary observables and let $\rho$ be a positive
    45	semidefinite operator of trace one.  We distinguish the state-dependent
    46	operator distance from the distance between their associated binary projective
    47	measurements:
    48	\begin{align*}
    49	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    50	    &:= \Re\tr\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big), \\
    51	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    52	    &:= \sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}
    53	      \Re\tr\big((P_S^s-P_T^s)^\dagger
    54	                       (P_S^s-P_T^s)\rho\big),
    55	  \qquad P_S^\pm := \frac{\Id\pm S}{2}.
    56	\end{align*}
    57	The normalization and correlation identities are
    58	\begin{align}
    59	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2 &= \frac12 d_\rho(S,T)^2,
    60	    \tag{normalization}\label{eq:normalization}\\
    61	  d_\rho(S,T)^2
    62	    &= 2-2\Re\tr(ST\rho),
    63	    \tag{operator correlation}\label{eq:operator-correlation}\\
    64	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    65	    &= 1-\Re\tr(ST\rho).
    66	    \tag{binary correlation}\label{eq:binary-correlation}
    67	\end{align}
    68	Consequently, the conclusion delivered by the quantum linearity argument can
    69	be written either as
    70	\[
    71	  \mathbb E_a\dbin_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq\delta
    72	\]
    73	or, equivalently, as
    74	\[
    75	  \mathbb E_a d_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq2\delta.
    76	\]
    77	These are not equivalent to the same bound $\delta$ for the mean squared
    78	state-dependent operator distance.%
    79	\footnote{The formal declarations are \leanid{binaryObservableEffect},
    80	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq},
    81	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_stateDepDistSq\_div\_two},
    82	\leanid{stateDepDistSq\_eq\_two\_sub\_two\_mul\_correlation}, and
    83	\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_one\_sub\_correlation} in
    84	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity/BooleanFourier.lean}.}
    85	
    86	\section{The source calculation}
    87	
    88	Natarajan and Vidick define the distance between two POVMs by summing the
    89	squared state-dependent distances between corresponding square roots
    90	\cite[Section~3.1]{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  For projective measurements the
    91	square roots are the effects themselves.  In the binary case their calculation
    92	expands $P_S^\pm=(\Id\pm S)/2$ and obtains
    93	\[
    94	  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
    95	    = 1-\frac12\tr_\rho(ST+TS)
    96	    = \frac12\tr_\rho((S-T)^2).
    97	  \tag{source equation (3)}
    98	\]
    99	This is equation~(3) at lines~903--910 of the in-repository source mirror.%
   100	\footnote{See
   101	\path{references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex}, lines~866--912.  The quantum
   102	linearity theorem and its Fourier--Naimark proof are at lines~1074--1112.}
   103	The next line identifies the final expression with the squared state-dependent
   104	operator distance.  The operator-distance definition at lines~873--875 is
   105	printed with $\rho$ occurring twice,
   106	\[
   107	  d_\rho(S,T)^2 = \tr_\rho\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big),
   108	  \qquad \tr_\rho(X) := \tr(\rho X),
   109	\]
   110	and we read the duplication as typographical, keeping the single $\rho$ of the
   111	definition of $d$ above.  Under that reading the squared state-dependent
   112	operator distance is $\tr_\rho((S-T)^2)$ rather than one half of that
   113	quantity.  Thus the calculation through line~910 is correct and the equality
   114	on line~911 loses a factor of two.
   115	
   116	The Fourier--Naimark proof is consistent with the measurement normalization.
   117	It proves
   118	\[
   119	  \mathbb E_a\operatorname{CON}_{\rho'}(A(a),\mathcal A(a))
   120	  = \frac12+\frac12\mathbb E_{a,b}
   121	       \tr_\rho(A(a)A(b)A(a+b)).
   122	\]
   123	The hypothesis therefore makes the consistency deficit at most $\delta/2$.
   124	For binary projective measurements, the squared measurement distance is twice
   125	that deficit, giving the bound $\delta$ for the squared binary-measurement
   126	distance and the bound $2\delta$ for the squared state-dependent operator
   127	distance.
   128	
   129	\section{A four-point counterexample}
   130	
   131	The bound $\delta$ for the mean squared state-dependent operator distance is
   132	false.  Let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$, choose $r\in G\setminus\{0\}$, take
   133	the one-dimensional state $\rho=1$, and define scalar binary observables by
   134	\[
   135	  A(a)=\begin{cases}
   136	    -1,&a=r,\\
   137	     1,&a\neq r.
   138	  \end{cases}
   139	\]
   140	For the characters $\chi_u(a)=(-1)^{u\cdot a}$, the normalized Fourier
   141	coefficients satisfy
   142	\[
   143	  \widehat A(0)=\frac12,
   144	  \qquad
   145	  \widehat A(u)=-\frac12\chi_u(r)\quad(u\neq0).
   146	\]
   147	Their multiset is
   148	$\{\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12\}$, and hence
   149	\[
   150	  \mathbb E_{a,b}A(a)A(b)A(a+b)
   151	    =\sum_u\widehat A(u)^3=\frac14.
   152	\]
   153	The correlation hypothesis therefore holds with $\delta=3/4$.
   154	
   155	Every scalar exact Boolean representation is one of the characters $\chi_u$,
   156	and its mean squared state-dependent operator distance from $A$ is
   157	\[
   158	  \mathbb E_a |A(a)-\chi_u(a)|^2
   159	    =2-2\widehat A(u)\geq1.
   160	\]
   161	Allowing an ancillary space does not reduce this lower bound.  Exact linearity
   162	and the binary-observable relations make the operators $\mathcal A(a)$ a
   163	commuting family of Hermitian involutions.  Their simultaneous spectral
   164	subspaces carry characters of $G$.  Evaluation in any density operator is

     6	This file proves the quantum linearity theorem of Natarajan and Vidick in the

    11	distance weighted by `ρ ⊗ |anc⟩⟨anc|`, to an exactly linear family of binary

    23	\section{At a glance}
    24	
    25	\begin{itemize}
    26	  \item \textbf{Difficulty: easy.}  No step of the retained proof route is
    27	  in doubt.  The obstruction is that the error function claimed in the
    28	  statement of the combined-lines lemma of the Pauli basis analysis,
    29	  $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is not delivered by either of the two
    30	  derivations printed in its source proof: one route establishes
    31	  $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, the other would give
    32	  $m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and rests in addition on a distributional
    33	  decomposition that the stated sub-line lemma does not supply.  The
    34	  correction is to state the first route's established error form and confirm
    35	  that the sole consumer tolerates it.
    36	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs:} the
    37	  Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for state-dependent operator distances
    38	  (project-local, blueprint Chapter 12), mixture decompositions of
    39	  question distributions, and elementary averaging over restricted
    40	  line distributions; no new Mathlib surface beyond finite
    41	  expectations and inner-product estimates already used by the

    43	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} a \textbf{statement-level error-form

    49	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split:} essentially \textbf{100\%

    52	  probability on finite sets.
    53	  \item \textbf{Key inputs:} the combined point and line measurements and
    54	  the sub-line distribution of the Pauli basis analysis in
    55	  \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, and the error function of the classical soundness
    56	  theorem imported from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, into which the

    60	
    61	\section{Key theorem forms}
    62	
    63	Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple of the Pauli basis
    64	test, $\ket{\hat\psi}$ is the expanded state of the projective strategy
    65	under analysis, succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, and all
    66	approximations are with respect to $\ket{\hat\psi}$.  For lines
    67	$\ell_X, \ell_Z$ in $\F_q^m$, the POVM $\{T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\}$,
    68	with outcomes pairs of polynomials of degree at most $md$ on the two
    69	lines, is the two-basis combined line measurement, and
    70	$\{\hat Q^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ is the combined point measurement; their
    71	consistency errors are $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and
    72	$\delta_Q = \poly(\eps)$ respectively, and
    73	$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}} = \poly(\eps)$ is the line--point consistency
    74	error of the strategy.  The lemma under discussion asserts that a
    75	measurement $\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, built for each line $\ell$ in
    76	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, is $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$-consistent, on average over
    77	the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, with the combined point
    78	measurement on the extended coordinates, together with the
    79	register-swapped counterpart.%
    80	\footnote{In the mirror of the source consulted here,
    81	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}: the
    82	lemma statement, with the error form $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is at
    83	lines~1020--1034 (label \path{lem:qld-4-13}); the central display with
    84	the first-route bound at lines~1134--1137
    85	(label \path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}); the three claims at
    86	lines~1140--1239 (labels \path{claim:17-1}--\path{claim:17-3}); the
    87	second-route conclusion $O(m^2\delta_P)$ at lines~1241--1245, preceded by
    88	a duplicated sentence whose second copy carries a malformed reference;
    89	the product-distribution estimate invoked there at lines~1055--1061
    90	(label \path{eq:qld-xz-lines-restricted}); and the sub-line lemma at
    91	lines~1063--1116 (label \path{lem:qld-sublines}).}
    92	The comparison involves four forms of the error function
    93	$\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.
    94	\begin{enumerate}
    95	  \item \textbf{Source form.}
    96	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = \poly(m^2\eps,\, md/q)$.  This is the form
    97	  printed in the statement.  Neither printed derivation supports it.
    98	  \item \textbf{Established form (first route).}
    99	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}
   100	  = O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
   101	  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)$, a function of the form
   102	  $m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$.
   103	  \item \textbf{Second-route form (conditional).}
   104	  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = O(m^2 \delta_P)
   105	  = m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$, conditional on a joint-law
   106	  decomposition that the sub-line lemma, as stated, does not provide.
   107	  \item \textbf{Consumer requirement.}  The unique consumer, the
   108	  polynomial-pair lemma, feeds $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$ into an error
   109	  of the form
   110	  $a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ imported
   111	  from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}; any bound
   112	  $m^{O(1)} \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ is absorbed by enlarging $a$ and
   113	  shrinking $b$, so forms~2 and~3 both suffice downstream.
   114	\end{enumerate}
   115	
   116	\section{The source assertion and the two routes}
   117	
   118	The source proof in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} constructs $\hat Q^{\ell}_f$ by
   119	averaging, over a distribution $D$ on tuples $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$
   120	provided by its sub-line lemma, the pushforward of
   121	$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}$ along a combining map, and reduces the lemma to a
   122	bound on the scalar consistency defect
   123	\begin{equation}
   124	  \Lambda \,=\,
   125	  \E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   126	  \E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   127	  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   128	  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   129	  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   130	  \ket{\hat\psi}\,,
   131	  \tag{\path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}}
   132	\end{equation}
   133	in which the point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ is uniform on $\ell$ and the sum
   134	ranges over pairs of line polynomials.  The proof then bounds $\Lambda$
   135	twice, by different routes and with different results, and the printed
   136	record is internally inconsistent: the display introducing $\Lambda$
   137	asserts the first-route bound, while the closing lines assert the
   138	second-route bound as the operative one; the lemma statement claims a
   139	third form matching neither.
   140	
   141	\paragraph{The first route.}
   142	Three claims are chained.  The combined point measurement
   143	$\hat Q^{x,z}$ is replaced by the ordered product of the two point
   144	measurements at cost $\delta_Q^{1/2}$; the $X$-point factor is removed at
   145	cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$; and the remaining $Z$-point
   146	correlation is shown to be within
   147	$\sqrt{m}\,(\delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} + \eps^{1/4})$ of one.  The
   148	factors of $m$ enter through the mixture structure of the sub-line
   149	distribution: each restricted line distribution carries mixture weight
   150	$1/(2m)$ in the line-point distribution, so an average bounded by
   151	$\delta$ over the full distribution is bounded only by $2m\delta$ over a
   152	restricted component and by $4m^2\delta$ over a product of two
   153	components, and the Cauchy--Schwarz steps halve the exponents.  Chaining
   154	the claims gives
   155	\begin{equation*}
   156	  \Lambda \,=\, O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
   157	  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)
   158	  \,=\, m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)\,.
   159	\end{equation*}
   160	One intermediate assertion needs a harmless correction: the final line
   161	of the proof of the second claim asserts the bound
   162	$O(m^2 \delta_{\mathrm{Line}})$ for a consistency term that is close to
   163	one, rather than for its deficit.  Read as a bound on the deficit ---
   164	which is what the surrounding Cauchy--Schwarz argument requires and what
   165	the invoked line--point consistency provides after the mixture
   166	inflation --- the claim and its use are correct, with the square root of
   167	the deficit giving the stated cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$.
   168	
   169	\paragraph{The second route.}
   170	After the chain, the source restarts: it asserts that, by Property~2 of
   171	its sub-line lemma, $\Lambda$ is a mixture, over types
   172	$\mathrm{v}_1, \mathrm{v}_2 \in \{\mathrm{ALine}, \mathrm{DLine}\}$ and
   173	indices $i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, of terms
   174	\begin{equation*}
   175	  \E_{(\ell_X, x) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_1,i}}\
   176	  \E_{(\ell_Z, z) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_2,j}}
   177	  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   178	  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   179	  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   180	  \ket{\hat\psi}
   181	\end{equation*}
   182	over two \emph{independently} sampled restricted line-point pairs,
   183	bounds each term by $O(m^2\delta_P)$ using the restricted-distribution
   184	consequence of the two-basis line lemma, and concludes
   185	$\Lambda = O(m^2\delta_P)$.  The invoked decomposition concerns the
   186	\emph{joint} law of the pair $((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z))$, where $x$ and
   187	$z$ are the two blocks of the single point sampled on $\ell$.  Property~2
   188	of the sub-line lemma does not assert this joint law: it asserts the
   189	component-wise product law of the pair of \emph{lines}
   190	$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, and the conditional uniformity of each point on its
   191	line separately --- equivalently, the laws of the two pairs
   192	$((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z'))$ and $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, z))$ in which
   193	the \emph{other} point is resampled independently.  These marginal
   194	statements are exactly what the first route's claims consume, each
   195	involving one point at a time; the joint decomposition used by the
   196	second route is a strictly stronger property and is not established by
   197	the lemma it is attributed to.
   198	
   199	\section{Why neither route yields the stated form}
   200	
   201	The stated error form is $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, a function of the two
   202	quantities $m^2\eps$ and $md/q$ that vanishes as both vanish.  The
   203	first-route bound is not dominated by any such function: along the
   204	scaling $\eps = m^{-4}$ with $q/(md) \to \infty$, both $m^2\eps = m^{-2}$
   205	and $md/q$ tend to $0$, while the term $m\,\eps^{1/4} = 1$ does not.
   206	Hence the established derivation supports no bound of the claimed form.
   207	The second-route bound, even granting the missing decomposition, carries
   208	the separate prefactor $m^2$: writing $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$
   209	with some fixed positive exponents, the contribution
   210	$m^2 (md/q)^{c}$ is not dominated by any vanishing function of $m^2\eps$
   211	and $md/q$, as the scaling $\eps = 0$, $md/q = m^{-2/c}$ shows, and the
   212	$\eps$-contribution fails similarly for sublinear exponents.  Neither
   213	observation asserts that the \emph{conclusion} of the lemma is false for
   214	some error function of the claimed form; the defect is that the printed
   215	proof does not deliver it.
   216	
   217	For orientation, the algebraic identity
   218	$m\,\eps^{1/2} = (m^2\eps)^{1/2}$ shows what a derivation of the claimed
   219	$\eps$-dependence would need: a chain that loses only square roots in the
   220	$\eps$-type quantities \emph{after} the restricted-distribution
   221	inflation would produce terms of the shape $(m^2\eps)^{1/2}$.  The
   222	printed chain loses fourth roots, through two nested Cauchy--Schwarz
   223	steps applied to already square-rooted quantities, and its
   224	$md/q$-dependence enters as $m\,\delta_P^{1/4}$, which the claimed form
   225	cannot absorb.
   226	
   227	\section{Correction and alternative repairs}
   228	
   229	The following are candidate directions, with their open obligations; none
   230	of the routes below is claimed as established.
   231	
   232	\paragraph{Corrected error form (adopted).}
   233	The blueprint adopts
   234	$\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ --- concretely,
   235	the first-route bound --- as the operative error form.  The only consumer is
   236	the polynomial-pair lemma, whose imported error
   237	$a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ absorbs
   238	$m^{O(1)}$ prefactors by enlarging $a$ and shrinking $b$.  The blueprint proof
   239	records this absorption and the corrected deficit reading of the second claim.
   240	The remaining obligation is formal: prove the three chained estimates and the
   241	consumer bound with explicit constants.
   242

   247	procedure makes this plausible, since in each component the two pairs

   272	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   273	
   274	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} corrects the combined-lines lemma to
   275	the established error form $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$.  Its proof derives the
   276	first route and uses that bound in the sequel.  The
   277	three claims are stated as separate lemmas with the corrected deficit
   278	assertion for the second; the sub-line lemma states Property~2 at the
   279	level of the two marginal laws and expressly disclaims the joint
   280	conditional law of the two points, so the blueprint statement does not
   281	license the second route; and the polynomial-pair lemma's proof absorbs
   282	the $m$ prefactor into the constants of the imported soundness error.  A
   283	chapter remark summarizes the discrepancy and cites this note.%

   299	\section{Conclusion}
   300	
   301	There is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma, together with an
   302	intermediate inconsistency: the printed proof asserts two different
   303	bounds for the same consistency defect, the first-route bound
   304	$O(m(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} +
   305	\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}))$ and the second-route bound
   306	$O(m^2\delta_P)$, the second resting on a joint-law decomposition that
   307	the sub-line lemma as stated does not supply; and the error form claimed
   308	in the lemma statement, $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, follows from neither.
   309	The first route is sound after a harmless deficit correction in its
   310	second claim and establishes $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$.  The
   311	discrepancy is harmless downstream, since the sole consumer absorbs
   312	polynomial-in-$m$ prefactors into its constants.  The blueprint therefore
   313	uses the corrected first-route form and cites this note; strengthening the
   314	sub-line lemma to license the second route is optional, and no route to the
   315	printed form is currently known.  We do not assert that the printed form is
   316	false.

   866	\subsection{State-dependent distance measure and approximations}
   867	
   868	We make extensive use of a state-dependent distance
   869	between measurements that has been frequently used in the context of
   870	entangled-prover interactive proof systems (see
   871	e.g.~\cite{IV12,ji2015classical}). For $\rho$ a positive semidefinite matrix and $X$ any linear operator define
   872	$$ \Trho(X) = \Tr(\rho X).$$ 
   873	For any two operators $S, T$, define the
   874	\emph{state-dependent distance} between $S$ an $T$ on a $\rho$ as
   875	$$ \Drho(S, T) := \sqrt{\Trho\big( (S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big)}.$$
   876	Based on the state-dependent distance we define a distance between POVMs, given by
   877	summing the state-dependent distance between the square roots of the POVM elements.
   878	Let $\{M^a\}$ and $\{N^a\}$ be two POVMs
   879	with the same number of outcomes, indexed by $a$, and let
   880	$\ket{\psi}$ be a quantum state. Then the state-dependent distance between the POVMs
   881	$M$ and $N$ on $\rho$ is denoted as $\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})$ and
   882	defined as
   883	\begin{align*}
   884	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N}) = \Big(\sum_a \Drho\big(\sqrt{M^a}, \sqrt{N^a}\big)^2\Big)^{1/2}.
   885	\end{align*}
   886	While this notation is ambiguous (since the sum over outcomes is not explicitly
   887	indicated), context will always make it clear which notion of $\Drho$ is
   888	intended. We will also drop the square roots in the case of POVMs that are
   889	projective measurements.
   890	
   891	To simplify the notation, let $A^a = \sqrt{M^a}$ and $B^a =
   892	\sqrt{N^a}$. Then this distance can be rewritten as:
   893	\begin{align}
   894	  \Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2 &= \sum_a \Trho\big( (A^a - B^a)^2 \rho\big) \notag\\
   895	               &= 2 - \sum_a \Re \Trho\big( A^a B^a \big),\label{eq:dpsi-1a}
   896	\end{align}
   897	where we  used the fact that $A^a$ and $B^a$ are
   898	Hermitian and their squares sum to identity. If we specialize to the case of projective measurements
   899	with binary outcomes, we get the following relations (here $A =
   900	A^1 - A^{-1}$ and $B = B^1 - B^{-1}$
   901	are the observables associated to the measurements):
   902	\begin{align}
   903	\Drho(\sqrt{M}, \sqrt{N})^2  &= 2 - \Trho\big(A^{1} B^{1} + A^{-1} B^{-1} + B^{1} A^{1} + B^{-1}
   904	                 A^{-1}\big)  \nonumber \\
   905	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4} \Trho\big((\Id + A)(\Id + B)
   906	                 + (\Id - A)(\Id - B) + (\Id + B)(\Id + A)
   907	                 + (\Id  - B)(\Id - A)\big) \ket{\psi} \nonumber \\
   908	               &= 2 - \frac{1}{4}\Trho\big(4\Id + 2 AB + 2 BA\big)\nonumber \\
   909	               &= 1 - \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big(AB + BA\big)  \nonumber \\
   910	               &= \frac{1}{2} \Trho\big((A - B)^2\big)\label{eq:dist_observables}    \\
   911	                &= \Drho(A, B)^2. \nonumber
   912	\end{align}
